1.note: "Guides of the perplexed" is the title of Maimonides' Moreh Nevukhim, which al-Ḥarizi himself translated into Hebrew. Here the phrase means simply the teachers who lose their way in these crafts.

2.note: Lev 11:19 lists הַחֲסִידָה הָאֲנָפָה, the stork and the heron, side by side. חֲסִידָה also means "pious (woman)", as in the line before; אֲנָפָה sounds like אנף, "be angry". The pious woman becomes an angry one.

3.note: A pun that cannot be carried over: תְּהִלָּה, praise, becomes תָּהֳלָה, folly or error (Job 4:18), a word with almost the same letters.

4.note: לֶחֶם הַפָּנִים, the showbread, is literally "bread of the faces". The letter has two faces, a forward one and a backward one. The next lines play on the showbread "before the LORD" and the showbread "taken away from before the LORD" (1 Sam 21:7).

5.note: The letter (lines from here to "May our lord never perish!") is built so that it can be read word by word from the last word to the first. Read so, each verb takes the noun that stood before it, and every praise becomes a curse. It starts: "Our lord, forever may he perish; may his Creator not grant him grace; ... may He cut off those who know him, and help his enemies, and subdue those who love him, and exalt his adversary ... and bring low his friends ... and remove his glory ... may his light and his lamp go out ... disgrace without kindness, blemish without beauty, rebellion without piety ... he loves backslidings, loathes what is fitting, pursues riches, hates uprightness, wraps himself in folly ... head of our reproach, who ends our greatness, renews our grief, puts our joy to flight, stirs up our sighing, takes away our honour, makes great our pain (צִיר also means pang), our lord." The forward text is translated here; the reversed sense is only in this note.

6.note: The same word twice: חֶסֶד is kindness, and also disgrace (Lev 20:17, Prov 14:34). Forward, "kindness without disgrace"; reversed, "disgrace without kindness".

7.note: "So-and-so" (פלוני) stands for the prince's name, which the author leaves out. יִצְּרֵהוּ, "may He guard him", has the letters of יוֹצְרֵהוּ, "his Maker". In the reversed reading אַל, "not", from the next line comes before it: "may his Maker not guard him".

8.he: גְּבִירֵנוּ לָנֶצַח יֹאבַד אַל יַמְצִיאֵהוּ. חֶסֶד בוֹרְאֵהוּ
8.note: These are the last words of the letter, "May his Creator grant him grace! May our lord never perish!", read in reverse order. The word אַל, "not", which forward goes with "perish", now goes with "grant".

9.note: The two lines of praise below are the same words, in reverse order, as the two lines of blame after them. Line 1 reversed is line 1 of the second poem, and line 2 reversed is its line 2.

10.note: Here חֶסֶד is read as disgrace (Lev 20:17), the same word that is "kindness" in the forward poem. שִׁמְצָה, "taint", is a rare word (Exod 32:25).

11.note: A play on two words with nearly the same letters: עֵבֶר, Eber, the ancestor of the Hebrews, and עֲרָב, Arabia, the Arabs. The east and west of the line before are the Jews of the Islamic East and of Spain and the West.

12.note: עֵרֶב is the woof of a fabric (שְׁתִי וָעֵרֶב, warp and woof, Lev 13:48). It is also a pun on עֲרָב, Arabic: the reader who knows both tongues has the whole fabric of both.

13.note: A pun on the name: חֶבֶר (Ḥever) and מְחַבֵּר, composer, literally "joiner".

14.note: מִנְגִידֵי is read as "for princes" (מִן with נְגִידִים), in contrast with "my foes" in the second half. "From the noble words of my mouth" is also possible. The line is the gate in small: the same words bless and curse.

15.note: A pun that cannot be carried over: תִיגַע, you will toil, and תִגַּע, you will touch (reach). The next words are from Exod 20:23, the altar that may not be climbed by steps; here, do not climb to my rank.

16.note: The raven of parting is the ghurāb al-bayn of Arabic poetry, the bird whose cry foretells the separation of friends.
